title: Race and Ethnicity: First Principles
description: What sociologists mean by race and ethnicity, and what calling them socially constructed does and does not claim

concepts.title: Two Words, Two Kinds of Grouping
concepts.contentHtml:
Start with the two words this topic is about. Sociologists usually use race for groupings based on perceived physical differences, such as skin colour, that people link to ancestry from particular parts of the world. Racial labels are often assigned by others before anyone claims them, and historically they have been ranked. Ethnicity refers to groupings based on shared culture and origin: language, religion, customs, a homeland, a story of common descent. Ethnic labels are more often claimed from within.

Max Weber gave the classic definition of the second idea. He called ethnic groups "those human groups that entertain a subjective belief in their common descent", a belief rooted in similarities of physical type or custom, or in memories of colonisation and migration.1 Then he added the twist: "it does not matter whether or not an objective blood relationship exists." What makes an ethnic group is the shared belief and what people do with it, not a verified pedigree. (Weber's wider sociology belongs to the classical theory topic; here you only need this definition.)

In practice the two ideas blur. Britain's Office for National Statistics (ONS) admits that there is no consensus on what constitutes an ethnic group, and that membership is self-defined.2 Its census list mixes colour ("White", "Black"), continents ("Asian", "African") and nations ("Indian", "Pakistani") in a single question, as Lesson 4 shows.

One consequence surprises many newcomers: majorities have an ethnicity too. In the 2021 census of England and Wales, 74.4% of residents chose "English, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish or British" as their ethnic group.3 Being in the majority makes an ethnicity feel like the default, the unmarked case, rather than like no ethnicity at all. Studying that unmarked default is part of the sociology of ethnicity too.

concepts.title: What 'Socially Constructed' Means
concepts.contentHtml:
You will often hear that race is socially constructed. The phrase packs three separate claims together, and it helps to pull them apart.

  • The categories are made. Which traits count as racial, how many races there are and where the boundaries fall come from history, law and politics rather than from biology alone. As the philosopher Michael Root notes, a person ascribed as Black in the United States would likely not be considered Black in Brazil, because the two countries divide people up differently.1 In 1930 American census takers were told to count anyone of mixed Black and white ancestry as Black "no matter how small the percentage of Negro blood".
  • The meanings are made. The stereotypes, prestige and suspicion attached to each category are produced and reproduced by institutions, media and everyday interaction.
  • The consequences are real. Constructed categories still shape who is hired, policed or segregated, so they produce measurable inequality.

Notice what the thesis does not say. It does not say that human bodies are all alike or that ancestry is a fiction; people do differ genetically, and the next lesson looks at exactly how. The claim is about the mapping: how a continuous spread of human variation gets sorted into a few named boxes, and what the boxes are then used for.

Nor does constructed mean unreal. Money and national borders are constructed too, and they are very real in their effects. The philosopher Paul Taylor put the point against sceptics: races, even if biologically unreal, remain real social objects.2 That is why sociologists who reject biological race still collect racial data. You cannot measure discrimination against a group you refuse to name. Whether naming a group also helps keep the category alive is one of the arguments you will meet in later lessons.

concepts.title: Do Races Exist? Three Answers
concepts.contentHtml:
If biological race in the old sense is false, does anything called race exist? The philosopher Ron Mallon's map of the debate divides serious answers into three camps, and each comes with a different policy instinct.

  • Racial scepticism. Anthony Appiah and Naomi Zack argue that the word race cannot refer to anything real, because the only thing it could pick out, discrete biological races with shared essences, does not exist.1 Both also adopt eliminativism, which recommends discarding the concept altogether.
  • Constructivism. Races are real, but as social kinds. Sally Haslanger defines racialised groups by three conditions: members are observed or imagined to have bodily features taken as evidence of ancestry from certain regions; those features mark them as occupying a subordinate or privileged position; and this plays a part in their systematic subordination or privilege. On this view race is as real as the hierarchy it organises. Haslanger is not a conservationist, though: she worries about embracing racial identities for the long term.
  • Population naturalism. Some biological grouping might deserve the name, provided nobody treats it as discrete or essential. Robin Andreasen defends cladistic races, lineages that split as human groups became isolated. Philip Kitcher suggested that laws against intermarriage might have created a genetically isolated African American population. Quayshawn Spencer argues that the five race categories of the US Office of Management and Budget map onto five "human continental populations" identified by population genetics.2

Every camp faces the same difficulty: drawing sharp lines through gradual variation. Most of this topic works with the constructivist answer, because sociology studies race mainly as a social relationship, but keep the other two in view. Lesson 2 gives you the genetic evidence each side appeals to.

title: Genes, Clines and Clusters
description: What human genetic variation does and does not show, from Lewontin's 1972 apportionment to genomic medicine

concepts.title: Lewontin's Apportionment
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1972 the geneticist Richard Lewontin asked a simple question: how is human genetic diversity divided up? He took data from 17 genetic "systems", protein variants such as blood groups that the methods of the day could detect, measured in populations around the world.1 He sorted those populations into seven races, along lines typical of the time, and used a measure of diversity based on Shannon entropy, borrowed from information theory, to split the total into parts.

The result became one of the most quoted numbers in the social sciences. At an average locus, 85.4% of human diversity lay within populations, 8.3% among populations within the same race, and only 6.3% among races.2 Most of the variation that exists anywhere in the species exists inside every population. Lewontin drew a blunt conclusion: since racial classification was "of virtually no genetic or taxonomic significance", no justification could be offered for its continuance.

The core finding has held up. Lewontin's 17 markers were few and possibly unrepresentative, but as human genetics moved to far larger datasets, later studies obtained similar figures. In 2002 Noah Rosenberg and colleagues analysed 377 markers in 1,056 people from 52 populations. Differences among individuals within populations accounted for 93 to 95% of genetic variation, and differences among major groups for only 3 to 5%.3

Be precise about what the number measures. It describes how variation at a typical locus is apportioned, and it implies that knowing someone's racial label tells you little about their genotype at any single gene. It does not, by itself, settle every question you might ask about ancestry, and that is where the argument went next.

concepts.title: Lewontin's Fallacy? Clusters and Clines
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2003 A. W. F. Edwards published a critique with a provocative title: "Human genetic diversity: Lewontin's fallacy". His point was that small differences at single loci are correlated across many loci, and added together they can reveal where a person's ancestors lived. Rosenberg's 2002 study showed this in practice. A clustering program given no information about where people came from found six main genetic clusters, five of which corresponded to major geographic regions.1

Who was right? Both, because they answered different questions. One question is how variation is apportioned among groups; the other is whether a genome can be used to infer ancestry. A 2007 study by geneticists at the University of Utah showed how the two fit together. With 10 loci, two people from different populations are more alike than two from the same population nearly a third of the time; with 1,000 loci, about 10% of the time; with many thousands of loci and geographically separated populations, never.2 Classification methods, which pool information across loci, can approach 100% accuracy with as few as 100. A 2022 review co-written by Rosenberg concludes that Edwards correctly identified a statistical error, but one that Lewontin himself did not make.3

A second argument concerns clines, gradual changes across space. Serre and Pääbo found in 2004 that when people are sampled evenly across the globe, allele frequencies change in gradients across the whole world rather than jumping at continental borders.4 Rosenberg's team replied in 2005, using 993 markers, that the clusters were not an artefact of sampling: they arise from small jumps in genetic distance across geographic barriers, while people from intermediate places have mixed membership.

So genetic structure is real, mostly gradual and slightly lumpy at major barriers. None of that turns a folk category such as "Hispanic", or the different meanings of "Black" in the United States and Brazil, into a biological unit.

concepts.title: Race, Ancestry and Medicine Now
concepts.contentHtml:
Outside population genetics, these arguments matter most in medicine, and researchers genuinely disagree.

In 2002 Risch and colleagues argued in Genome Biology that an epidemiological perspective strongly supports the continued use of self-identified race and ethnicity in biomedical research. Rosenberg's team made a more cautious point the same year: self-reported ancestry can help assess epidemiological risks but does not remove the need for genetic data in studies of genes and disease.

Since then, official guidance has moved the other way. In 2023 a committee of the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine urged researchers to avoid using race as a proxy for human genomic variation, since race is a social construct, and to avoid typological thinking: the assumption that people fall into distinct, fixed and ranked groups. The report still treats race as an appropriate descriptor for some purposes, such as studying the effects of racism on health.1 In March 2024 editors of major journals, including JAMA and Nature Genetics, adopted guidance that race, ethnicity and geographic origin should no longer be used as proxies for genetic ancestry groups in genomic science.2

Clinical practice has changed in places too. In September 2021 a task force of the National Kidney Foundation and the American Society of Nephrology, set up to reassess the inclusion of race in diagnosing kidney disease, recommended a 2021 equation that estimates kidney function without a race variable.3

Keep measurement and interpretation apart. Nobody in this debate denies that ancestry varies or that some variants differ in frequency between populations. The dispute is whether a social category is a good stand-in for ancestry, and whether relying on it hides the environmental and social causes of health gaps, including racism itself.

title: How Racial Categories Were Made
description: Colonial law, natural history and eugenics: how modern racial categories were built, ranked and later disowned

concepts.title: Virginia Writes Race into Law
concepts.contentHtml:
Racial categories have birthdays, and some of them are written in statute books. Colonial Virginia relied on two kinds of bound labour: servants, bound for a term of years, and slaves, bound for life. Writing in 1705, Robert Beverley summed up the distinction: "Slaves are the Negroes, and their Posterity [children], following the condition of the Mother". Each part of that sentence had been made by law.

In 1662 Virginia legislated the doctrine of partus sequitur ventrem, which assigned a child's status as free or slave according to the status of the mother.1 Slavery became hereditary, passed down through women, whoever the father was.

The 1705 Act concerning Servants and Slaves went further. Imported servants who were Christians and of Christian parentage would serve a fixed term. Those who were not Christians in their native country were to be slaves, and remain so even if they converted to Christianity afterwards; baptism no longer freed anyone.2 The same act forbade a master to "whip a Christian white servant naked without an order from a justice of the peace".3 The word white now marked a legal status with its own protections.

Look at the logic. At first the boundary followed religion, which a person could change. Once conversion stopped counting, the boundary followed birth and descent, which nobody can change. A line drawn by faith was redrawn as a line drawn by ancestry and colour.

Historians still argue about cause and effect: whether settlers' prejudice produced racial slavery, or whether a slave economy produced the prejudice that justified it. Either way, the Virginia statutes show the constructivist claim from Lesson 1 in its plainest form. The category was not discovered in nature; a legislature defined it and courts enforced it.

concepts.title: Natural History Ranks Humanity
concepts.contentHtml:
In the eighteenth century European naturalists set out to classify humanity as they classified plants. Johann Friedrich Blumenbach (1752–1840), sometimes considered the father of modern anthropology, identified four varieties of mankind in his 1775 dissertation, added a fifth in 1781, and in 1795 first coined the term Caucasian for the peoples of Europe, West Asia and northern India.1 He chose the name because he claimed this variety originated in the Caucasus mountains of Georgia, and he justified the claim by the superior beauty he saw in Georgians. His other labels were Mongolian, Ethiopian, American and Malay.

The nineteenth century tried to measure the hierarchy. The physician Samuel George Morton measured the cranial capacity of hundreds of skulls from different races. In 1978, and later in The Mismeasure of Man, the biologist Stephen Jay Gould argued that Morton had unconsciously skewed his data to fit his preconceptions, and Morton became a textbook example of scientific racism.

Then the story turned. In 2011 a team of anthropologists relocated and remeasured 308 of the 670 skulls whose capacity Morton had published, and found that only 7 of them (2%) differed significantly from his figures.2 They concluded that Morton had not manipulated his data, and that Gould, who never measured the skulls himself, was the biased one. Weisberg replied in 2014 that most of Gould's arguments were sound, though overstated in places.3 Kaplan, Pigliucci and Banta argued in 2015 that both sides missed the deeper problem: Morton's groups were in many cases not populations in any biologically meaningful sense, so no analysis of his data could answer the interesting questions.4

That last point is the one to keep. Accurate measurement does not rescue a badly posed question. A skull can be measured correctly and a racial ranking built on it can still be worthless.

concepts.title: Eugenics and the Retreat from Biological Race
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1883 the English statistician Francis Galton, a cousin of Charles Darwin, coined the word eugenics for "the study of agencies under social control that may improve or impair the racial qualities of future generations either physically or mentally." Within decades it had become law.

American eugenicists declared certain people unfit or "feebleminded", and laws in 30 states led to the involuntary sterilisation of at least 60,000 people by the 1970s.1 Those targeted were disproportionately Latinos, Native Americans, African Americans, poor white people and disabled people. In Buck v. Bell (1927) the Supreme Court upheld the sterilisation of Carrie Buck, whom the opinion called a "feeble-minded white woman"; Justice Holmes wrote that "three generations of imbeciles are enough." Eugenicists also helped pass the 1924 Johnson-Reed Act, which completely excluded immigrants from Asia.2 Nazi Germany took the logic furthest: at least 400,000 forced sterilisations, the killing of at least 70,000 adults and 5,200 children deemed unworthy of life, and genocide.

The scientific challenge came from inside anthropology. Franz Boas attacked a cornerstone of racial typology, cranium size, by showing that it was profoundly affected by environment: American-born children of immigrants tended to have larger crania than their European-born parents. After the war, a 1950 UNESCO statement denied the biological foundations of race, although it took until 1996 for the American Association of Physical Anthropologists to publish a similar document.3

Two lessons follow. First, eugenics was not a fringe: it drew in experts from many disciplines and flourished in the three decades before the end of the Second World War, and practices such as involuntary sterilisation persisted in many states until at least the 1970s. Second, heredity was used to rank people by class and disability as well as by colour, which is why a poor white woman became its test case in the Supreme Court.

title: Counting Race: The Census Question
description: How the US and British censuses ask about race and ethnicity, and why changing the question changes the count

concepts.title: Two Centuries of the US Race Question
concepts.contentHtml:
The US census has asked about race since 1790, and it has rarely asked the same question for long. Each version records what the state wanted to know, and who had the power to decide.

The first census, in 1790, had only three racial categories: free whites, all other free persons and slaves.1 "Mulatto" was added in 1850. In 1890 enumerators had to distinguish mulattoes, defined as having "three-eighths to five-eighths black blood", from quadroons and octoroons; officials dropped these categories in 1900, judging the data "of little value and misleading". In 1930 enumerators were told to count anyone who was both Black and white as Black, "no matter how small the percentage of Negro blood": the census version of the one-drop rule.

Other groups were moved between boxes. Until 1930 Mexicans had been classified as white. A "Mexican" race category appeared in the 1930 census, but Mexican Americans, helped by the Mexican government, lobbied successfully to eliminate it in 1940 and to be classified as white again, which gave them more legal rights.2 A person counted as Asian Indian since 1980 could have been recorded as Hindu in 1920 to 1940, as "other race" in 1950 and 1960, and as white in 1970.3

Two reforms changed the question itself. Beginning in 1960, Americans could choose their own race rather than have it assigned by an enumerator. Since 2000 they have been able to choose more than one. The 2010 census therefore had 63 possible race categories, six single races and 57 combinations, and 2.9% of Americans (9 million) chose more than one.

Read in sequence, the census is less a mirror held up to the population than a record of shifting theories about it, from blood fractions to self-identification. That is why sociologists read census categories as evidence about the society that wrote them.

concepts.title: Britain's Ethnic Group Question
concepts.contentHtml:
Britain came to the question two centuries later and framed it differently. Since 1991 the census for England and Wales has asked about ethnic group, and the list has been updated at every census since.1

  • 2001 offered four Mixed options, such as White and Black Caribbean, alongside a separate Irish category within White.
  • 2011 moved Chinese from the "Other" group into "Asian" and added Gypsy or Irish Traveller and Arab.2
  • 2021 added Roma and a write-in box for Black African.

The question has two stages: you choose one of five high-level groups, then one of 19 options, some with space to write in. The 2021 results show a changing country. In all, 81.7% of residents identified as White, down from 86.0% in 2011, and 74.4% as White British, down from 87.5% in 2001.3 The Asian group, at 9.3% of the population, saw the largest rise. The new Roma box was ticked by 101,000 people, and within "Other White" there were 614,000 Polish and 343,000 Romanian residents. The ONS warns that such changes reflect ageing, fertility, mortality and migration, but may also come from differences in how people chose to self-identify between censuses.4

Now look at the logic of the list. It mixes colour (White, Black), continent (Asian, African), nation (Indian, Pakistani) and way of life (Gypsy or Irish Traveller). Scotland's 2022 census list even includes "Polish" and "Showman or Showwoman". These are not slips. Each box answers a practical question about who needs to be counted, for equality monitoring or for a community that asked to be seen, and that is exactly what racial formation theory, in Lesson 6, would predict.

concepts.title: When Changing the Question Changes the Count
concepts.contentHtml:
In August 2021 the US Census Bureau reported that the multiracial population had grown from 9 million in 2010 (2.9% of the population) to 33.8 million in 2020 (10.2%), a 276% increase.1 Headlines spoke of a multiracial boom. The Bureau was more careful: it said the differences were largely due to improvements in the design of the two separate questions on race and Hispanic origin and in data processing and coding, as well as some demographic change.2

Other numbers moved in step. The "White alone" population fell by 8.6%, while the number reporting White in combination with another group rose by 316%. "Some Other Race", meant as a residual box, reached 49.9 million people alone or in combination, overtaking the Black population as the second-largest race group, and 93.9% of those choosing Some Other Race alone were Hispanic.

Individuals move too. At least 9.8 million Americans gave a different race or Hispanic-origin answer in the 2010 census than in the 2000 census, especially people of multiracial background.3

In March 2024 the Office of Management and Budget revised its standards. Federal agencies must now collect data with a single combined race and ethnicity question that allows multiple answers, add Middle Eastern or North African as a category separate from White, and collect detailed groups by default. The change drew on the Bureau's 2015 National Content Test of 1.2 million housing units. Not everyone agreed: some commenters warned that many Afro-Latinos would tick only Hispanic or Latino and be undercounted, and that a combined question implied Hispanic is a race.4

This is the general lesson about separating measurement from interpretation. A change in a count can reflect a change in the population, in the question, or in how people choose to answer it. Before you read any trend in racial or ethnic data, ask which of the three you are looking at.

title: Du Bois, Chicago and the Assimilation Model
description: Du Bois's empirical sociology and double consciousness, and the Chicago school's assimilation cycle and its modern heirs

concepts.title: Du Bois in the Seventh Ward
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1896 the University of Pennsylvania hired W. E. B. Du Bois, who the year before had become the first Black person to receive a PhD from Harvard, to study the Black population of Philadelphia's Seventh Ward. The result, The Philadelphia Negro (1899), combined archival research, extensive observation and door-to-door surveys. Du Bois sat in the parlours, kitchens and living rooms of 2,500 Black households, and the book included a colour-coded map showing the social class he assigned to each household he visited.1

The commission came with expectations. The philosopher Lewis Gordon argues that the study's sponsors set Du Bois up to present Blackness itself as the problem, rather than to understand the problems Black people faced. Mapping the ward household by household, class by class, was itself a reply: it treated Black Philadelphia as a varied community rather than a single type.

In 1897 Du Bois moved to Atlanta University, where he edited the Atlanta University Studies from 1898 to 1914.2 In The Scholar Denied (2015) the sociologist Aldon Morris argues that this work made Atlanta the first empirically oriented school of sociology in the United States, and that some of its best studies, such as The Negro Artisan (1902), came before the most celebrated works of the Chicago school.3 Morris argues that academic racism kept this record from being recognised.

Not every reader accepts the whole claim. Reviewing the book, Monica Bell agreed that the Atlanta school did empirical research before Chicago, but objected that empiricism alone does not constitute sociology, which also needs theory, and that the discipline's founding was too fragmented for a single origin story.4 The dispute is about Du Bois, and also about how a discipline decides whom to count as its founders.

concepts.title: The Colour Line and Double Consciousness
concepts.contentHtml:
In The Souls of Black Folk (1903) Du Bois made two moves that still shape the field. The first was structural and global. "The problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color line," he wrote in the book's forethought, and he defined that line as "the relation of the darker to the lighter races of men in Asia and Africa, in America and the islands of the sea."1 The colour line was not only an American arrangement but a world order.

The second move was about experience. White acquaintances, Du Bois wrote, circled around a question they never asked outright: "How does it feel to be a problem?" His answer was double consciousness, "this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity." One feels "two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings" in one body.2

Double consciousness is not only a wound. Du Bois described a longing to merge the double self into a better and truer self in which neither older self is lost. He would not Africanize America, and he would not bleach his Negro soul in a flood of white Americanism; he wanted it to be possible to be both a Negro and an American. Philosophers still dispute the content and significance of the concept.

Later, in Black Reconstruction (1935), Du Bois added a political economy of race. He argued that whiteness gave white workers a public and psychological wage that compensated them for low economic wages, and that it formed the basis of a cross-class political alliance between white workers and employers against Black workers.3 That argument anticipates a question sociologists still ask: why racial division can outweigh shared class interests.

concepts.title: Park's Cycle and Its Heirs
concepts.contentHtml:
The other founding tradition came from the University of Chicago. Robert E. Park (1864–1944) proposed a race relations cycle, the first systematic attempt to explain how relations between groups begin and evolve.1 When groups first come into contact, through immigration or conquest, relations tend to be competitive and conflictual. They settle into accommodation, a working arrangement, and they end in assimilation, which Park defined as "a process of interpenetration and fusion in which persons and groups acquire the memories, sentiments, and attitudes of other persons or groups".

The cycle fits some histories well. European immigrants who arrived between the 1820s and 1920s faced intense rejection, yet their descendants assimilated and reached parity with national norms in jobs and income; researchers describe white ethnic identity as being in its "twilight". It fits relations between Black and white Americans badly. One reading treats slavery and then legal segregation as two long accommodations, followed since the 1960s by renewed conflict, without assimilation. Critics also fault the theory for saying little about how long assimilation takes or how it actually happens.2

The live question concerns the immigrants who have arrived since the 1960s. Portes and Rumbaut argue for segmented assimilation: some groups will assimilate not into the mainstream but into a marginalised urban underclass. Other analysts answer that this view amounts to blaming the victim, and point to steady assimilation by generation. Language is one test. The share of the second generation speaking only English at home ranged from 8% among Dominicans to almost 80% among Filipinos; in the third generation it ranged from 50% among Dominicans to almost 100% among Japanese and Filipinos.3

Notice the hidden premise. Assimilation needs a mainstream to assimilate into, and the cycle treats that mainstream as neutral. Racial formation theory, in the next lesson, starts by questioning exactly that.

title: Racial Formation and Critical Race Theory
description: How race is made through racial projects, and the legal movement that became a political battleground

concepts.title: Racial Formation: Race as a Project
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 1980s many sociologists felt that older approaches treated race as something else in disguise: a kind of ethnicity on its way to assimilation, or a cover for class. Michael Omi and Howard Winant's Racial Formation in the United States, first published in 1986, offered an influential alternative. They define racial formation as "the sociohistorical process by which racial categories are created, inhabited, transformed, and destroyed", and insist that race is a matter of both social structure and cultural representation.1

The engine of the process is the racial project, which in their words "is simultaneously an interpretation, representation, or explanation of racial dynamics, and an effort to reorganize and redistribute resources along particular racial lines."2 The census boxes of Lesson 4 are racial projects; so were the 1930 "Mexican" category and the campaign that removed it. On a smaller scale, so is a landlord's judgement about a tenant's name. Race, on this view, is never settled; it is continually made and contested.

One influential extension describes what happened after the civil rights era, when open racism lost respectability. Eduardo Bonilla-Silva's theory of colour-blind racism holds that racial inequality is now upheld and rationalised through frames such as these:3

  • Abstract liberalism: using ideas of equal opportunity and individual choice in a way that ignores structural inequality.
  • Naturalisation: treating racial patterns, such as segregation, as natural and inevitable.
  • Victim blaming: explaining inequality by presumed cultural deficiencies of minority groups.
  • Minimisation: downplaying ongoing discrimination.

Be clear about what kind of claim this is. The frames are an interpretation of how people talk and reason about race. Whether a given appeal to equal treatment is a frame that shields inequality or a sincere principle is exactly what critics dispute, as the last concept in this lesson shows.

concepts.title: Critical Race Theory: Born in the Law Schools
concepts.contentHtml:
Critical race theory (CRT) is often discussed today as if it were a school curriculum. It began somewhere else. The movement developed in the mid-1970s, as lawyers, law students and legal scholars sympathetic to the social justice movements of the 1960s witnessed a backlash against the advances of the previous decade.1 Its roots ran through critical legal studies, which treated law as an instrument for maintaining the status quo rather than a set of abstract rational principles, and through the civil rights and Black Power movements and radical feminism. The first CRT conference was held in Madison, Wisconsin, in 1989.2

Two ideas show its style. Derrick Bell, who with Alan Freeman made up the first generation of CRT scholars, coined interest convergence: there will be no racial progress unless the interests of the marginalised align with the interests of those in power. In a 1980 Harvard Law Review essay he asked why the Supreme Court struck down school segregation in Brown v. Board of Education, and offered explanations beyond justice, including the credibility the decision gave America in its struggle with communist countries to win the hearts and minds of emerging third world people.3

The second idea came from Kimberlé Crenshaw, whose 1989 article "Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex" offered a Black feminist critique of anti-discrimination doctrine and gave the field the term intersectionality: race and sex can combine to produce disadvantages that neither category captures alone.4 The gender topic takes this idea further.

CRT scholarship is diverse. Some authors use personal narrative or fiction as argument; others use conventional social science. Much of it argues about how legal doctrines, including colour blindness, should be interpreted or changed. Keep that origin in mind: CRT was a set of arguments among lawyers about law long before it became a slogan in school-board politics.

concepts.title: Arguing About Critical Race Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Few academic ideas have generated as much political heat, so take the positions one at a time, each in its strongest form.

The case for. Defenders such as Rashawn Ray of the Brookings Institution summarise the core claim like this: US social institutions, from the criminal justice system to schools, labour and housing markets and healthcare, are laced with racism embedded in laws, rules and procedures that lead to different outcomes by race. On this reading CRT does not attribute racism to white people as individuals; it asks how formally neutral rules can still reproduce racial inequality.1

The case against, on method. In Beyond All Reason the legal scholars Daniel Farber and Suzanna Sherry argued that "radical multiculturalists", critical race scholars among them, attack traditional concepts of objective truth, reason, merit and the rule of law, and prefer storytelling to rigorous analysis.2 Other critics have said that personal narratives figure too centrally while empirical data is minimal, and that CRT diagnoses inequality but offers few answers on how to address it.3 Nancy Levit replied that such critiques tend to caricature their targets.4

The case against, on principle. Many critics hold that the cure for racial classification is to stop classifying. When the US Supreme Court struck down race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina in 2023, the majority wrote: "Eliminating racial discrimination means eliminating all of it." Justice Sotomayor answered in dissent: "Ignoring race will not equalize a society that is racially unequal."5

The politics. By November 2021 a Brookings assessment of anti-CRT state legislation counted nine states that had passed such laws, although none of the bills actually mentioned the words "critical race theory".6

These disagreements are of different kinds. Some are about evidence (how much discrimination exists, which Lesson 7 measures), some about method (what counts as knowledge), and some about values (whether equal treatment means ignoring race). Data can settle the first kind, but not the last.

title: Measuring Discrimination, Disparity and Contact
description: Field experiments on hiring, Britain's divergent ethnic gaps, and what meta-analyses say about intergroup contact

concepts.title: Emily, Greg, Lakisha and Jamal
concepts.contentHtml:
Gaps in outcomes do not by themselves prove discrimination, since groups may differ in qualifications, location or choices. To isolate discrimination, researchers run field experiments, also called correspondence or audit studies: send employers matched applications that differ only in a signal of race, and count the replies.

The best known is by Marianne Bertrand and Sendhil Mullainathan, published in 2004. They answered help-wanted adverts in Boston and Chicago newspapers with fictitious résumés, each randomly given a very African American sounding name or a very white sounding one. White names received 50% more callbacks for interviews.1 A higher-quality résumé brought 30% more callbacks for white names but a far smaller increase for Black names, and employers who advertised themselves as Equal Opportunity Employers discriminated as much as the rest.

Is it getting better? In 2017 Quillian and colleagues pooled every available US field experiment on hiring discrimination against African Americans or Latinos: 28 studies, 55,842 applications for 26,326 positions. Since 1989, white applicants received on average 36% more callbacks than African Americans and 24% more than Latinos.2 They found no change over 25 years in discrimination against African Americans, and only modest evidence of a decline for Latinos.3 Many people assume discrimination has steadily fallen; at the point of hire, this evidence says it has not.

In a study first circulated in 2021, Patrick Kline, Evan Rose and Christopher Walters sent more than 83,000 applications to jobs at 108 of the largest US employers. Distinctively Black names reduced the probability of contact by 2.1 percentage points, and the gap was highly concentrated: firms in the top fifth for discrimination accounted for nearly half of the contacts lost by Black applicants.4

Know the limits. These studies measure first contact, not hiring, pay or promotion, and a name can signal class as well as race. They are strong evidence that discrimination happens at that stage, and say little on their own about how much of a later pay gap it explains.

concepts.title: Britain's Gaps Point Different Ways
concepts.contentHtml:
If you expect every minority group to trail the majority, British data will surprise you. In England's GCSE results for 2022 to 2023 the average Attainment 8 score was 46.3 out of 90. Chinese pupils scored highest (65.5), followed by Indian pupils (59.4).1 Bangladeshi (51.9), Black African (48.7) and Pakistani (47.0) pupils also scored above White British pupils (44.9), while Black Caribbean pupils averaged 40.0 and Gypsy or Roma pupils 20.3, the lowest of all.

Pay shows a similar spread. ONS analysis for 2012 to 2022 found that Chinese and Indian employees had higher earnings than White British employees, while Bangladeshi and Pakistani employees earned less.2 Adjusting for qualifications, occupation, age and geography changes the picture: the Chinese gap shifts the most, Indian employees born outside the UK go from earning more than White British employees to earning less, and UK-born Black African and Black Caribbean employees consistently earned less.

How to read such patterns is fiercely contested. The government's Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities, chaired by Tony Sewell, concluded in 2021: "we no longer see a Britain where the system is deliberately rigged against ethnic minorities."3 It argued that geography, family influence, socio-economic background, culture and religion have more impact on life chances than racism. The report drew criticism from many quarters, including the charge that it denied institutional racism, which Sewell rejected.4

Field experiments add a different kind of evidence. In a 2019 study for Nuffield College's Centre for Social Investigation, Valentina Di Stasio and Anthony Heath sent fictitious applications to nearly 3,200 real jobs. Applicants from minority ethnic backgrounds had to send 60% more applications to get a positive response than white British candidates, and Black Britons and people of Pakistani background faced discrimination at levels unchanged since the late 1960s and 1970s.5

Both findings can hold at once: many minority groups outperform the majority at school, and employers still discriminate against minority applicants. Outcome gaps and discrimination measure different things.

concepts.title: Does Contact Reduce Prejudice?
concepts.contentHtml:
The social psychology topic introduced Allport's contact hypothesis: prejudice falls when groups meet under equal status, common goals, cooperation and institutional support. The sociological question is how strong the evidence is.

The landmark is Pettigrew and Tropp's 2006 meta-analysis of 713 independent samples from 515 studies.1 It found that intergroup contact typically reduces intergroup prejudice; that the finding did not appear to result from participant selection or publication bias; that more rigorous studies showed larger effects; and that effects usually generalised to the whole outgroup. Allport's conditions strengthened the effect, but they turned out not to be essential.2

Most of those studies, though, were not experiments, and people who seek out contact may already be less prejudiced. In 2019 Elizabeth Levy Paluck, Seth Green and Donald Green kept only studies with random assignment and delayed outcome measures. There were just 27. Their results were consistent with contact typically reducing prejudice, but interventions aimed at ethnic or racial prejudice produced substantially weaker effects, and they found no such studies addressing adults' racial or ethnic prejudices.3

A field experiment in Iraq shows both the promise and the limit. Mousa randomly assigned Iraqi Christians displaced by the Islamic State to an all-Christian football team or to a team mixed with Muslims. Christians with Muslim teammates became more likely to vote for a Muslim player from another team to receive a sportsmanship award, to register for a mixed team the next season, and to train with Muslims six months later. The effect did not carry over to other settings, such as visiting a restaurant in Muslim-dominated Mosul, and attitudes did not change consistently.4

The fair summary: contact reliably changes how people treat the particular others they meet, and often how they feel about the wider group. Turning it into lasting reductions in racial prejudice among adults remains a well-supported hope rather than a proven policy.
